claims.text: The baseline system is a pure elemental Cr coating deposited directly on zirconium-alloy cladding.
An ultrathin Al interlayer, exemplified as less than 100 nm thick, is to be inserted between the Zr substrate and Cr coating.
Al is a suitable design addition for improving the performance of accident-tolerant coatings in high-temperature steam.
The buried Al interlayer will oxidize during high-temperature steam exposure.
Oxidation of the Al interlayer will form a continuous, dense, adherent Al2O3 barrier at the Cr/Al interface.
The Al2O3 barrier will inhibit diffusion of Cr into Zr and diffusion of Zr in the opposite direction.
The Al2O3 barrier will remain stable under normal PWR primary-water conditions.
Stability of the barrier under normal PWR conditions will maintain the coating's corrosion resistance.
Compared with a directly deposited Cr coating, the Al-interlayer coating will have significantly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Compared with the baseline, the Al-interlayer coating will delay coating failure during high-temperature steam oxidation.
Compared with the baseline, the Al-interlayer coating will preserve or improve corrosion resistance during subcritical-water operation.
Elemental Cr coatings can peel and crack during high-temperature steam oxidation.
Approximately 300°C is the relevant normal-operation PWR primary-water test temperature.
Transient steam exposure up to approximately 1000°C is an accident-relevant test boundary.
Normal-water testing should use extended exposure, whereas accident-relevant steam testing should use shorter transient exposure.

A lack of statistically significant reduction in Cr–Zr interdiffusion depth together with a lack of improved high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
